exercises.name: Dead bug
how_to: Lie on your back with your knees bent above your hips and your shins parallel to the floor.
Reach both arms straight up toward the ceiling, directly above your shoulders.
Press your lower back gently into the floor so there is no gap under your waist.
Breathe out and slowly lower your right arm overhead while straightening your left leg toward the floor.
Stop before your lower back lifts. Breathe in and return to the start.
Alternate sides, moving slowly enough that the movement takes about four seconds each way.
exercises.spoken_instruction: Dead bug. Knees above hips. Extend the opposite arm and leg slowly, keeping your lower back down.
safety_notes: Stop lowering the leg the moment your lower back arches away from the floor.
Keep your neck relaxed; if it strains, rest your head on a folded towel.
common_mistakes: Letting the lower back arch, which shifts the work off the deep abdominals.
Rushing the movement so momentum carries the limbs rather than control.

exercises.name: The hundred, preparation
how_to: Lie on your back, knees bent above your hips, arms long by your sides.
Curl your head, neck and shoulders slightly off the mat, looking toward your knees.
Hold your arms just off the floor and pulse them up and down in small movements.
Breathe in for five pulses and out for five pulses.
Keep your ribs drawing down toward your hips throughout.
exercises.spoken_instruction: The hundred. Curl your shoulders off the mat and pulse your arms, five counts in, five out.
safety_notes: If your neck tires, lower your head to the mat and keep pulsing the arms.
Keep the curl small; height is not the point.
common_mistakes: Pulling on the neck to lift higher.
Holding the breath instead of using the five-count rhythm.

exercises.name: Shoulder bridge
how_to: Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet flat, hip-width apart.
Press through your heels and peel your hips off the mat one vertebra at a time.
Stop when your hips, knees and shoulders form a straight line.
Hold for two breaths, then lower slowly from the top of the spine down.
exercises.spoken_instruction: Shoulder bridge. Press through your heels and lift your hips, then lower one vertebra at a time.
safety_notes: Do not push the hips higher than a straight line; over-arching loads the lower back.
Keep your knees tracking over your ankles rather than falling inward.
common_mistakes: Lifting with the lower back instead of the glutes.
Letting the knees splay apart at the top.

exercises.name: Side plank from the knees
how_to: Lie on your side with your bottom forearm on the mat, elbow under your shoulder, and your knees bent behind you.
Stack your hips and shoulders so your body forms one line from head to knees.
Lift your hips away from the floor and hold, breathing evenly.
Lower with control and change sides.
exercises.spoken_instruction: Side plank from the knees. Elbow under your shoulder, lift your hips into one straight line and hold.
safety_notes: Keep the supporting shoulder pressed down and away from your ear.
Come down if the shoulder or wrist starts to ache.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips drift backward so the line breaks at the waist.
Sinking into the supporting shoulder.

exercises.name: Single leg stretch
how_to: Lie on your back and curl your head and shoulders slightly off the mat.
Draw one knee toward your chest and hold your shin, extending the other leg away at about 45 degrees.
Switch legs smoothly, keeping your torso still and your ribs drawing down.
Breathe out as each knee comes in.
exercises.spoken_instruction: Single leg stretch. Curl up, draw one knee in and extend the other leg away, then switch smoothly.
safety_notes: Extend the moving leg higher if your lower back lifts off the mat.
Support your head with one hand if your neck fatigues.
common_mistakes: Rocking the torso side to side as the legs change.
Dropping the extended leg so low that the back arches.

exercises.name: Reformer footwork, toes
how_to: Lie on the carriage with your head on the headrest and the balls of your feet on the footbar, heels together and toes apart.
Set a moderate spring load, typically two to three springs depending on your reformer.
Press the carriage away by straightening your legs, stopping just short of locking the knees.
Return slowly, letting the springs resist rather than pull you back.
exercises.spoken_instruction: Reformer footwork on the toes. Press the carriage away, stopping short of locking your knees, and return slowly.
safety_notes: Check the springs are attached before you load the carriage.
Keep your heels lifted and together; do not let the ankles roll outward.
common_mistakes: Snapping the knees straight at the end of the press.
Letting the carriage return faster than you can control.

exercises.name: Reformer leg circles in straps
how_to: Lie on the carriage with both feet in the straps and legs extended at about 45 degrees.
Use a light spring load so the work comes from your control rather than the springs.
Circle both legs outward and around, keeping your pelvis completely still.
Complete the set, then reverse the direction.
exercises.spoken_instruction: Leg circles in the straps. Circle both legs outward, keeping your pelvis still, then reverse.
safety_notes: Make the circles smaller if your pelvis rocks or your back arches.
Keep the straps under tension throughout so they cannot snap slack.
common_mistakes: Circling so wide that the lower back lifts.
Gripping the shoulders up toward the ears.

exercises.name: Elliptical steady state
how_to: Stand tall on the pedals with a light hold on the handles.
Set a resistance you can sustain while still able to speak in full sentences.
Keep a steady cadence and let your heels stay in contact with the pedals.
Aim for an effort of three to four out of ten.
exercises.spoken_instruction: Elliptical steady state. Settle into a pace you could hold a conversation at, around three to four out of ten.
safety_notes: Do not lean your body weight onto the handles; it reduces the work and strains the wrists.
Ease off if you feel light-headed.
common_mistakes: Choosing a resistance so low that the pedals carry you.
Bouncing the shoulders with each stride.

exercises.name: Elliptical hard interval
how_to: Raise the resistance one or two steps above your steady-state setting.
Drive the pedals with a strong, quick cadence.
Target an effort of eight to nine out of ten, where speaking is limited to a few words.
Hold the effort for the full interval, then drop back to an easy pace to recover.
exercises.spoken_instruction: Hard interval. Lift the resistance and drive hard, eight to nine out of ten.
safety_notes: Build up to hard intervals over two to three weeks rather than starting here.
Stop immediately if you feel chest pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness.
common_mistakes: Going so hard in the first interval that later ones collapse.
Cutting the recovery short, which flattens the whole set.

exercises.name: Seated flat road
how_to: Set the saddle so your knee stays slightly bent at the bottom of the pedal stroke.
Sit tall with your hands resting lightly on the bars.
Add enough resistance that the flywheel feels connected rather than spinning freely.
Hold a smooth cadence of roughly 80 to 90 revolutions per minute.
exercises.spoken_instruction: Seated flat road. Sit tall, smooth cadence around eighty to ninety.
safety_notes: Never pedal with no resistance; the flywheel will drive your legs faster than you can control.
Keep your knees tracking forward, not bowing outward.
Stop if you feel chest pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness.
common_mistakes: Saddle set too low, which loads the front of the knee.
Gripping the bars hard enough to hunch the shoulders.

exercises.name: Seated climb
how_to: Increase the resistance until the cadence naturally drops to around 60 to 70.
Stay seated, hinge very slightly forward from the hips and keep your torso quiet.
Push through the whole pedal circle rather than stamping down.
Hold an effort of six to seven out of ten.
exercises.spoken_instruction: Seated climb. Add resistance and drive through the whole pedal stroke.
safety_notes: Reduce resistance if your hips start rocking side to side.
Keep breathing rhythmically; do not hold your breath through the hard part.
Stop if you feel chest pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness.
common_mistakes: Pulling on the bars to compensate for too much resistance.
Letting the cadence fall below 55, which grinds the knees.

exercises.name: Standing sprint
how_to: Keep a moderate resistance — enough to stand against, not so much that you stall.
Rise out of the saddle with your hips over the pedals and hands on the wide part of the bars.
Drive a fast, controlled cadence at an effort of nine out of ten.
Sit back down and spin easy as soon as the interval ends.
exercises.spoken_instruction: Standing sprint. Out of the saddle, fast and strong, nine out of ten.
safety_notes: Do not stand with light resistance; you will lose control of the pedals.
Skip this movement entirely if you have knee or hip pain today.
Stop if you feel chest pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness.
common_mistakes: Bouncing the hips rather than staying centred over the pedals.
Holding the sprint past the point where form breaks down.

exercises.name: March in place
how_to: Stand tall and march on the spot, lifting each knee to about hip height.
Swing your arms naturally in opposition to your legs.
Build gradually from a walking pace to a brisk one over the interval.
exercises.spoken_instruction: March in place. Lift the knees and let the arms swing, building the pace gradually.
safety_notes: Hold a wall or chair if your balance is unsteady.
common_mistakes: Starting too fast, so the warm-up becomes the workout.

exercises.name: Supine knee hug
how_to: Lie on your back and draw both knees gently toward your chest.
Hold behind your thighs rather than over the front of your knees.
Breathe slowly and let your lower back settle into the mat.
Hold for the full interval without bouncing.
exercises.spoken_instruction: Supine knee hug. Draw both knees toward your chest and breathe slowly.
safety_notes: Ease off to a comfortable stretch; this should never be sharp.
common_mistakes: Pulling hard on the front of the knee joint.
